# Signed exponentials, largest-coefficient merging, and a simplex cap gap

This note proves a scalar inequality. It does not assert a mixed-integer
centerpoint theorem. All exponential random variables below are independent
and have density `exp(-t) 1_{t>0}`.

## 1. A conditional-mean lemma

Let `Z_i=c_i E_i`, with finitely many nonzero real coefficients `c_i`, at
least one positive and at least one negative. Write

`S=sum_i Z_i`, `mu=sum_i c_i`, and `c_+=max_i c_i>0`.

The density `f` of `S` is positive on the whole real line. For every `i`,
the conditional mean

`m_i(s)=E[Z_i | S=s]`

has a continuous version that is nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz. Moreover,

`sum_i m_i(s)=s` for every real `s`.

Proof. Each signed exponential density is log-concave on its halfline
support, and their convolution is log-concave. Here we use the standard
convolution consequence of the Prekopa-Leindler theorem, with densities
extended by zero outside their supports. Let `g_i` be the density of the
sum of the coordinates other than `i`. It is log-concave, including when
that sum has one-sided support. The unnormalized conditional density is

`h_s(z)=r_i(z) g_i(s-z)`,

where `r_i` is the signed exponential density of `Z_i`. Log-concavity gives,
for `s_1<s_2` and `u<v`,

`h_{s_2}(v)h_{s_1}(u) >= h_{s_2}(u)h_{s_1}(v)`.

This cross-product formulation remains valid at zeros of either density
and therefore handles moving support endpoints without taking undefined
likelihood ratios. Multiplying by `v-u`, integrating over `u<v`, and
dividing by `f(s_1)f(s_2)` proves `m_i(s_2)>=m_i(s_1)`.

The densities `g_i` are bounded. Exponential tails of `r_i` consequently
dominate the zeroth and first conditional-moment integrals locally
uniformly in `s`. Translation continuity of the convolution integrals
(or dominated convergence away from the finitely many possible one-phase
boundary discontinuities) gives continuous versions of both integrals.
Since `f(s)>0`, the conditional means are continuous. The identity
`sum_i m_i(s)=s` first holds almost everywhere by conditioning and then
everywhere by continuity. Thus, for `s_1<s_2`, the nonnegative increments
`m_i(s_2)-m_i(s_1)` sum to `s_2-s_1`; each is at most that number. This
proves the Lipschitz assertion. In particular, almost everywhere,

`m_i'(s)>=0`, and `sum_i m_i'(s)=1`. QED.

## 2. A signed-exponential mode bound

With the preceding notation, `f` is nondecreasing on
`(-infinity,mu-c_+]`. In particular, at every differentiability point
`s<mu-c_+`, one has `f'(s)>=0`.

Proof. Define the continuous, locally Lipschitz, strictly positive function

`tau(s)=sum_i c_i m_i(s)
       =sum_i c_i^2 E[E_i | S=s]`.

The previous lemma yields `tau'(s)<=c_+` almost everywhere. Exponential
integration by parts gives, for each smooth compactly supported test
function `phi`,

`E[(Z_i-c_i) phi(S)]=E[c_i Z_i phi'(S)]`.

This identity has the same sign for negative `c_i`: both expressions on
the right before conditioning equal `c_i^2 E[E_i phi'(S)]`. Summing and
conditioning proves, in the distributional sense,

`(tau f)'=(mu-s)f`.

The density `f` is continuous (it is a convolution of at least two
integrable bounded densities). The displayed identity makes `tau f`
continuously differentiable. Since `tau` is positive and locally
Lipschitz, `f` is locally absolutely continuous, and almost everywhere

`tau(s) f'(s)=(mu-s-tau'(s))f(s)
             >=(mu-s-c_+)f(s)`.

It follows that `f'>=0` almost everywhere below `mu-c_+`; absolute
continuity proves the stated monotonicity. No uniqueness or attainment of
a mode is needed. QED.

## 3. Merging a largest positive coefficient

Let `a_1,...,a_p>0`, `b_1,...,b_q>0`, with `p>=2`, `q>=1`, and
`sum_i a_i=sum_j b_j`. Put

`P(a,b)=Pr(sum_i a_i E_i >= sum_j b_j F_j)`.

Suppose `a_i` is a largest positive coefficient and `j!=i`. For
`0<=t<=a_j`, replacing `(a_i,a_j)` by `(a_i+t,a_j-t)` cannot increase
`P`, where a zero coefficient at the endpoint is omitted.

Proof. First take `0<=t<a_j` and use the current coefficients in the
following formulas. Let

`V=sum_i a_i E_i-sum_j b_j F_j`.

Differentiation under the expectation is legitimate: the density of the
negative sum is bounded, and the differentiated integrand is dominated
by a constant times `E_i`. Exponential size bias gives

`partial_{a_i} P=f_{V+a_i E_i'}(0)`.

Indeed, size bias replaces `E_i` by a sum of two independent unit
exponentials. Let

`W=V+a_i E_i'+a_j E_j'`.

Convolution with a positive exponential of mean `c` obeys
`c f_W'+f_W=f_{W-cE'}`. Applying this first with `c=a_j`, then with
`c=a_i`, and subtracting gives exactly

`partial_{a_i}P-partial_{a_j}P=(a_j-a_i) f_W'(0)`.

The sum defining `W` has at least four positive exponential phases, so
its density is continuously differentiable, including at zero. For
clarity, the convolution of four positive exponential densities, extended
by zero on the negative halfline, is continuously differentiable with
bounded derivative; convolution with the remaining densities preserves
this property.

Assume now that the sums of the original positive and negative
coefficients agree. Then the mean of `W` is `a_i+a_j`, and its largest
positive coefficient is `a_i`. Section 2 therefore makes its density
nondecreasing up to `a_j>0`; in particular `f_W'(0)>=0`. Since
`a_i>=a_j`, the derivative along the transfer is nonpositive. The same
argument applies throughout the transfer, since the receiving
coefficient remains largest. At `t=a_j`, almost sure convergence and the
absence of an atom at equality give continuity of `P`.

Thus the merging assertion is proved when the positive and negative
coefficient sums agree. No unrestricted merging assertion for unequal
sums is intended. QED.

## 4. The scalar sharp inequality

Let `a_i,b_j>0`, with `sum_i a_i=sum_j b_j=1`. Then

`Pr(sum_i a_i E_i >= sum_{j=1}^q b_j F_j)
 >= (q/(q+1))^q`.

Proof. If there is more than one positive coefficient, repeatedly merge
another coefficient into a largest one. Section 3 shows that this can
only decrease the probability. At the end the positive sum is a single
unit exponential, so

`P >= E exp(-sum_j b_j F_j)=prod_j(1+b_j)^(-1)`.

Arithmetic-geometric mean and `sum_j b_j=1` give
`prod_j(1+b_j)<=(1+1/q)^q`. Equality in the stated scalar inequality is
attained with one positive coefficient and all negative coefficients
equal to `1/q`. QED.

## 5. Centroid caps of a simplex

Let `T` be a `d`-simplex and let a halfspace, proper relative to `aff(T)`,
have boundary through its centroid. Let `q` be the number of vertices strictly on the excluded
side. Then its relative volume is at least `gamma_q`, where
`gamma_q=(q/(q+1))^q` for `q>=1`.

Proof. Let `v_0,...,v_d` be the values of the defining affine functional
at the simplex vertices, with the included halfspace corresponding to a
nonnegative functional value. The centroid condition gives `sum_i v_i=0`.
Properness implies that both positive and negative values occur. A
uniform point of `T` has barycentric coordinates
`E_i/(sum_j E_j)`: this follows by the change of variables from positive
exponentials to their sum and their simplex proportions, whose Jacobian
is the `d`th power of the sum. Therefore the cap fraction is

`Pr(sum_{v_i>0} v_i E_i >= sum_{v_i<0} (-v_i)E_i)`.

Zero values are irrelevant. The positive and negative coefficient sums
agree; divide both by their common sum and use Section 4. QED.

In particular, if a closed centroid cap contains at least two vertices,
then `q<=d-1`, and its volume fraction is at least `gamma_{d-1}` for
`d>=2`. Vertices on the boundary count as contained. The numbers `gamma_r`
decrease with `r`: differentiating `r log(r/(r+1))` gives
`-log(1+1/r)+1/(r+1)<0`. Thus zero vertex values and smaller negative
vertex counts only improve this bound.

## 6. Scope of the merging rule

Merging two arbitrary positive coefficients is false, even when both
coefficient sums equal one. For

`X=(E_1+E_2+18E_3)/20`, `Y=(F_1+F_2)/2`,

the exact probability is `30094/65219`. Merging the first two coefficients
gives `X'=(2E_1+18E_2)/20` and probability `407/882`. The difference is

`Pr(X>=Y)-Pr(X'>=Y)=-25/1173942<0`.

The valid proof above always merges into a largest coefficient. The
counterexample is checked independently by the accompanying exact
fraction-arithmetic verifier; it is not used to prove the theorem.
